summary: A guide to the many SIP specifications, listing a snapshot of the documents under the SIP umbrella, briefly summarizing each, and grouping them into categories. This is an informational document.

plainLanguage.summary: SIP has a huge pile of instruction manuals. This is the table of contents that tells you which one to read for what.

questions: where to start learning sip specifications
subtitle: Navigate the many specifications that extend the Session Initiation Protocol

tldr.problem: SIP (Session Initiation Protocol) has become the subject of hundreds of specifications from the IETF. It can be difficult to find the right document or even to know which RFCs exist, since they are spread across many different functional areas.
tldr.mechanism: This document provides a snapshot of the SIP specification landscape as of early 2009. It lists nearly all RFCs related to SIP, groups them into topics such as core specifications, PSTN interworking, NAT traversal, security, conferencing, and instant messaging, and provides a brief description of each one.
tldr.outcome: Newcomers, implementors, and deployers can now navigate the SIP ecosystem more easily. The guide helps readers find the specifications relevant to their use case without having to search blindly.

today: RFC 5411 is an Informational document that provides a snapshot of SIP specifications as of January 2009. It was designed to guide newcomers and implementors through the expanding SIP ecosystem. Since publication, SIP specifications have continued to evolve. RFC 3261 remains the core protocol definition, though it has been updated by numerous clarifications and extensions.

sections.title: SIP and Its Specifications
sections.content:
Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) is the IETF standard for initiating multimedia sessions, most commonly used for voice calls over IP. RFC 3261 defines the core protocol. Since then, the IETF has produced dozens of extensions and related specifications to support PSTN gateways, security, conferencing, instant messaging, presence, emergency services, and many other capabilities.

This rapid growth makes SIP a sprawling landscape. Specifications define extensions to the protocol itself, add new MIME types for SIP bodies, extend the Session Description Protocol (SDP) for SIP use, and describe interworking between SIP and legacy telephone networks. Some are Standards Track, others are Informational or Experimental. A developer wanting to build a SIP application needs to know which specifications apply to their use case.

This document serves as a map. It groups SIP specifications into logical topic areas, describes what each specification does, and indicates whether it is Standards Track (S), Best Current Practice (B), Experimental (E), or Informational (I).
sections.plainLanguage: SIP is a way to start phone calls over the internet. There are so many add-on instructions for different jobs that it's hard to find the right one. This document lists them all and groups them by what they do.

sections.title: Core and Essential Specifications
sections.content:
The core specifications are those used for almost every SIP session, registration, or subscription. RFC 3261 is the protocol itself, often called the 'president of the galaxy' in this guide's lighthearted Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy references. RFC 3263 describes how to use DNS to find a SIP server from a SIP URI. RFC 3264 defines how SDP (Session Description Protocol) is used with SIP to negotiate media parameters through an offer/answer model.

RFC 3265 defines the SUBSCRIBE and NOTIFY methods, which form the foundation of SIP's event notification system. RFC 3265 is required whenever any event package is used, for features like presence and call state notifications.

Other essential specifications address problems found in deployments. RFC 3581 defines the rport parameter for symmetric response routing through NAT. RFC 3327 defines the Path header to allow inbound requests to traverse edge proxies. RFC 4474 provides cryptographic identity verification. GRUU (Globally Routable User Agent Identifier) allows directing requests to a specific device instance. OUTBOUND defines how to maintain TCP or TLS connections for receiving inbound requests when behind NAT.
sections.plainLanguage: The core rules are the ones you use for every call. They cover how to start a call, describe what kind of media you want, and handle common problems like being behind a firewall.

sections.title: Topic Areas and Extensions
sections.content:
Beyond the core, SIP has grown into several specialized domains. PSTN Interworking covers connecting SIP to the traditional telephone network, including specifications like SIP-T (which tunnels ISDN signaling), PINT (for third-party call control), and SPIRITS (for PSTN-to-IP queries).

General Infrastructure Extensions provide capabilities like reliable provisional responses (RFC 3262, PRACK), privacy and anonymity (RFC 3323), the INFO method for mid-dialog information, call history tracking (RFC 4244), and session timers for cleanup (RFC 4028).

NAT Traversal extends the core specifications with ICE (Interactive Connectivity Establishment) for media, TCP support for ICE, and outbound connection management.

Call Control Primitives enable features like third-party control and call transfer. The Event Framework and Event Packages build on SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY for presence, dialog state, and other subscriptions. Quality of Service specifications cover COPS integration and PSTN QoS mapping. Conferencing covers conference servers and ad-hoc conference setup. Instant Messaging, Presence, and Multimedia extend SIP for SIMPLE (SIP for Instant Messaging and Presence Leveraging Extensions). Emergency Services add location awareness and emergency routing.
sections.plainLanguage: Different parts of SIP handle different jobs. Some talk to old phone systems. Some handle secret calls. Some manage connections through firewalls. Some enable group chats and presence information.

sections.title: Security and Authentication
sections.content:
The Security Mechanisms section groups specifications that provide security functionality for SIP. These include mechanisms for authentication, encryption, and protection of SIP messages and user identities.

RFC 4474 (SIP Identity) provides a way to assert a calling party's identity cryptographically, enabling robust caller ID and blocking spam calls. RFC 3325 (P-Asserted-Identity) is a simpler, P-header mechanism widely deployed despite its limited-applicability status. RFC 3323 defines the Privacy header for requesting anonymity.

TLS support for SIP signaling, defined in the core specifications, protects the transport of SIP messages themselves. However, end-to-end encryption of SIP message bodies and media streams requires additional mechanisms, which are defined in security-specific extensions.

The guide notes that specifying and deploying security in SIP is complex because SIP necessarily involves many parties in a call: the caller, the callee, any proxies in between, and infrastructure servers like registrars. Protecting against insider threats at network operators and preventing call redirection attacks remain active research and standardization areas.
sections.plainLanguage: SIP security includes ways to prove who you are, hide your identity if you want, and encrypt the call. The tricky part is protecting calls when many servers are involved in routing them.

sections.title: Scope and Usage of Specifications
sections.content:
The guide defines what it means to be a 'SIP specification': RFC 3261 itself, any specification that extends RFC 3261, the SDP specification (RFC 4566) and extensions to SDP that support SIP, and any specification that defines a MIME type whose primary purpose is to support SIP.

Excluded are pure requirement documents, architecture frameworks, registry definitions, and processes. The guide does include Best Current Practices when they normatively describe mechanisms or provide significant guidance on usage, such as call flow examples.

The guide originally included Internet Drafts that were still under development, noting that final codepoint assignments might change before publication. It also notes that some specifications that were developed to solve problems later discovered to be insoluble (like overlap dialing in RFC 3578) remain specified with clear caveats about their limitations.

The document is presented as a 'work-in-progress' snapshot. The field of SIP specifications continues to evolve, with new extensions regularly created to support emerging applications and deployment scenarios. The guide itself is expected to be periodically updated as the SIP ecosystem matures.
sections.plainLanguage: This guide covers the official SIP rules from the IETF, which includes the main protocol, add-ons, and ways to format data. It doesn't include pure planning documents or temporary experiments, but it does include examples and best practices.
